rv.q: Whatever Stevens’s personal background, whatever the spiritual vocabulary of his writing, his art reaches for a sense of worship and possibility that eschews labels, limits, and exclusions.

And while my gut tells me the show — from New York City Ballet resident choreographer Justin Peck that’s set to the songs of Sufjan Stevens — is not really a musical per se, it is a transporting and soul-stirring experience all the same.
But with the verbal dials turned way down, and the physical and musical ones way up, the calibration of information, from dreamy to piercing, is pretty much perfect.
Illinoise is a gorgeous, ambitious work that succeeds in translating Stevens' introspective indie folk into something bigger and more communal
And Peck and Stevens, along with their collaborators and the "Illinoise" family, have given new life to a Broadway musical.
Nothing about this is typical Broadway fare, but that's exactly what makes it so worth seeing.
This has not been a banner year for new musicals on Broadway, but with “Illinoise,” the final show I saw this season, I glimpsed the majestic future.
Which feels appropriate given that for the Sufjan Stevens faithful — and maybe even for many casual fans or those unfamiliar with his music
The show is a gorgeous, sprawling meditation on love, loss and the search for meaning, told through dance that is both earthbound and transcendent.
Drury and Peck have crafted something cinematic, a true tribute to Stevens’s original brilliance.
It’s not a show for all tastes but it certainly makes the case that it belongs on Broadway.
Yet in all honesty, for all the obvious delight sprinkled over 'Illionise,' it did not move me.
Illinoise makes a striking case for how modern dance, set to contemporary music, can tell a story that speaks to generations of audiences without preaching or condescension.
It remains, above all else, a magical work of fierce heart that bursts with indescribable wells of emotion.
Illinoise is a show that succeeds on multiple levels, offering both visual and aural delights that complement each other beautifully.

Justin Peck’s folk ballet Illinoise, an eleventh-hour entry into this Tony Awards race (so late that its first preview and opening night were the same 2pm Wednesday matinee), is perhaps the most original new musical of the past year.
Perhaps he wants things precisely this way.
Illinoise is a wonderfully collaborative effort that raises the “barre” for Broadway musicals moving forward.
Another word to describe 'Illinoise' is 'simple-minded.'
It ought to be enjoyed for its beauty, melancholy, and simplicity.
This show is still dancing around inside me as I think about the effortless way these dancers uplift a heavy story.
It’s a full-bodied celebration of telling stories, being vulnerable, and (very loosely) Illinois making some noise right now at the St. James Theatre.
